subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The description of corporate governance as a system by which companies are directed and controlled, having to do with power and accountability, who exercises it, on whose behalf and how, is attributed to-

options.A: Adrian Cadbury
options.B: Milton Friedman
options.C: N. R. Narayana Murthy
options.D: Philip Kotler

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Adrian Cadbury.

Adrian Cadbury, who chaired the Cadbury Committee, described corporate governance as a system by which companies are directed and controlled, having to do with power and accountability. Milton Friedman put it in terms of conducting business in accordance with shareholder desire while observing the basic rules of society. The Narayana Murthy Committee emphasised the non-alienable rights of shareholders as true owners and the role of the directors as trustees.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under which theory of corporate governance are the directors regarded as stewards of the assets of the company, who decide what is to be done and drive the people of the company?

options.A: Trusteeship theory
options.B: Stewardship theory
options.C: Agency theory
options.D: Stakeholder theory

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Stewardship theory.

Stewardship theory treats directors as stewards of the assets of the company. Agency theory treats them as agents of the shareholders bound to run the company in the shareholders best interest. Stakeholder theory requires a balance to be kept between the interests of a wider body of stakeholders. Trusteeship theory rests on the relationship of trust arising because the shareholders have committed large sums to the directors judgment.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following correctly distinguishes ethics from corporate governance?

options.A: Ethics emerges naturally and applies at every level, while governance normally applies at the top level and has to be studied and experienced
options.B: Ethics is enforced by regulation and applies at the top level, while governance emerges naturally and applies at every level of the organisation
options.C: Ethics and governance are both regulated in most countries, the only real difference being that governance is confined to listed companies
options.D: Ethics relates to the method of governing a company, while governance relates to the inner self of the individual as reflected at the workplace

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Ethics emerges naturally and applies at every level, while governance normally applies at the top level and has to be studied and experienced.

Ethics consists of the values and principles which relate to the inner self of an individual and are reflected at the workplace; it emerges naturally and a manager has to be honest at every level. Corporate governance is the method of governance, normally applied at the top level because corporate policies and procedures are framed there, it has to be studied and experienced, and regulations matter because compliance is strict.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf
generation_source: Self-authored practice MCQ, based on ICMAI Study Material

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: In distinguishing management from corporate governance, the view taken is that-

options.A: in management the methodology matters more than the results, while in governance the result achieved is the only meaningful measure of performance
options.B: regulations are important in management because an organisation cannot frame its own rules, while governance is left wholly to the discretion of the Board
options.C: management and governance both emerge naturally with the situation, so that neither of them needs to be separately studied or experienced by a manager
options.D: in management the results matter more than the methodology, while in governance the methodology of achieving the result matters more than the result

answer_html:
Answer: (D) in management the results matter more than the methodology, while in governance the methodology of achieving the result matters more than the result.

Management emerges with the situation, its regulations are largely internal because an organisation can have its own rules subject to the law, and the results are treated as more important than the methodology of achieving them. Corporate governance has to be studied and experienced, regulation is important to it, and the methodology of achieving the result is treated as more important than the result itself.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is NOT among the stated objectives of corporate governance?

options.A: Achieving an ideal composition of the Board of Directors so as to justify independence in decision making
options.B: Reducing risk by following risk management through a process of due diligence within the organisation
options.C: Maximising the return to the equity shareholders in preference to the claims of the other stakeholders
options.D: Satisfying the stakeholders justifiably by balancing the conflict of interest amongst the stakeholders

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Maximising the return to the equity shareholders in preference to the claims of the other stakeholders.

The objectives are the justifiable satisfaction of stakeholders by balancing conflicting interests, transparent and logical policies, an ideal Board composition justifying independence of decision making now regulated under the Listing Regulations, optimum use of the resources of the company, risk reduction through due diligence, and a strong relationship of trust with stakeholders. Preferring the equity shareholders over the other stakeholders is the traditional profit-centred view which the shift from management to governance was intended to displace.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Clause 49 of the listing agreement, the first major corporate governance compliance required of listed companies in India, was based on the recommendations of the-

options.A: Narayana Murthy Committee
options.B: Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee
options.C: Rahul Bajaj Committee
options.D: K. R. Chandratre Committee

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee.

The Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee was set up by SEBI and its recommendations were carried into the listing agreement. It differed from the earlier committees in not treating the audit committee alone as the basis of corporate governance, and in separating its mandatory recommendations from its non-mandatory ones.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee recommended that an audit committee should consist of-

options.A: a minimum of five non-executive directors, every one of them independent of the management, at least two having financial and accounting knowledge, meeting twice a year
options.B: a minimum of two independent directors together with the finance director, at least one of the three having financial and accounting knowledge, meeting six times a year
options.C: a minimum of three non-executive directors, a majority of them independent, at least one having financial and accounting knowledge, meeting at least three times a year
options.D: a minimum of three directors of whom a majority are executive, at least one being a practising chartered accountant in whole-time practice, meeting at least four times a year

answer_html:
Answer: (C) a minimum of three non-executive directors, a majority of them independent, at least one having financial and accounting knowledge, meeting at least three times a year.

The recommendation was that an audit committee be set up to enhance the credibility of financial disclosures and promote transparency, with a minimum of three non-executive directors, a majority of them independent, at least one director having financial and accounting knowledge, and at least three meetings a year. The committee was also to investigate the reasons for financial defaults such as non-payment to depositors, debenture holders, shareholders and creditors.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: On the recommendation of the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee, a director may be a member of not more than-

options.A: ten committees across companies, and may chair not more than five of them
options.B: five committees across companies, and may chair not more than three of them
options.C: fifteen committees across companies, and may chair not more than ten of them
options.D: ten committees in a single company, and may chair not more than two of them

answer_html:
Answer: (A) ten committees across companies, and may chair not more than five of them.

The recommendation was that the directors of these committees cannot be members of more than ten committees across companies and cannot chair more than five committees. The limit is therefore counted across all the companies in which the director holds office, not company by company.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The committee constituted by the Confederation of Indian Industry under the chairmanship of Rahul Bajaj recommended that audit committees be set up by-

options.A: every listed company without any threshold at all, within one year of the recommendations being made public
options.B: listed companies with a turnover of ₹100 crore and paid-up capital of ₹20 crore, whichever is less, within two years
options.C: companies with a paid-up capital of ₹5 crore, the constitution of the committee being disclosed in the annual report
options.D: companies with a capital of ₹10 crore and a net worth of ₹25 crore, adherence being required by April 2000

answer_html:
Answer: (B) listed companies with a turnover of ₹100 crore and paid-up capital of ₹20 crore, whichever is less, within two years.

The Rahul Bajaj Committee recommended that only a listed company with a turnover of ₹100 crore and paid-up capital of ₹20 crore, whichever is less, should set up an audit committee within two years of reaching that threshold. The ₹5 crore paid-up capital test belongs to the K. R. Chandratre Committee, and the ₹10 crore capital with ₹25 crore net worth test to the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee's recommendation on the presence of independent directors on the Board was that-

options.A: half the directors should be independent in every case, whether the chairman of the Board is an executive or a non-executive chairman
options.B: one-third of the directors should be independent in every case, the character of the office held by the chairman being wholly immaterial
options.C: half the directors should be independent, but where the chairman is non-executive the outside directors may comprise one-third of the Board
options.D: one-third of the directors should be independent, but where the chairman is non-executive half the directors on the Board should be independent

answer_html:
Answer: (C) half the directors should be independent, but where the chairman is non-executive the outside directors may comprise one-third of the Board.

The recommendation was that half the directors in a Board should be independent, but where the chairman is non-executive the outside directors may comprise one-third of the directors. The committee also recommended that representatives of financial or investment institutions should not sit on the Board except in the case of default or potential default, and that such institutions should raise their voice as shareholders.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is NOT a duty of an independent director under Schedule IV to the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: To obtain the prior approval of the Board before seeking the opinion of an outside expert on a Board matter
options.B: To seek information and, where necessary, take and follow professional advice of outside experts at the expense of the company
options.C: To report concerns about unethical behaviour, actual or suspected fraud, or violation of the code of conduct of the company
options.D: To refrain from sharing unpublished price sensitive information unless the disclosure is approved by the Board or required by law

answer_html:
Answer: (A) To obtain the prior approval of the Board before seeking the opinion of an outside expert on a Board matter.

Schedule IV entitles an independent director to seek information and, where necessary, to take and follow appropriate professional advice and the opinion of outside experts at the expense of the company; no prior approval of the Board is required for that. The duties also include regularly refreshing his knowledge of the company, attending Board, committee and general meetings, participating constructively, not unfairly obstructing the functioning of the Board, reporting unethical behaviour or fraud, and preserving confidential and price sensitive information.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The International Finance Corporation defines a family business as a company in which-

options.A: the founder continues to hold the office of chairman or managing director, whatever the distribution of the voting rights may be
options.B: the whole of the paid-up share capital is held by the members of a single family and no person outside that family holds any share
options.C: the voting majority is in the hands of the controlling family, including the founders who intend to pass the business on to their descendants
options.D: at least one half of the directors are members of a single family, whatever the proportion of the voting rights that family may hold

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the voting majority is in the hands of the controlling family, including the founders who intend to pass the business on to their descendants.

The International Finance Corporation, an institution of the World Bank Group, defines a family business as a company where the voting majority is in the hands of the controlling family, including the founders who intend to pass the business on to their descendants. Its Family Business Governance Handbook records that in many countries family businesses represent more than 70 per cent of all businesses.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is NOT stated to be a feature of corporate governance in family owned companies in India?

options.A: Full time directors and senior management personnel are drawn from the family or are related to its members
options.B: Conflict of interest is common, the personal interest of the promoter conflicting with the interest of the company
options.C: Emotions are attached to the business, so decisions are sometimes taken which are not managerially correct
options.D: Compliance with the listing regulations is relaxed for a listed company which is owner or promoter managed

answer_html:
Answer: (D) Compliance with the listing regulations is relaxed for a listed company which is owner or promoter managed.

Corporate governance is highly regulated in India and the compliances are codified, so a listed family managed company must follow them exactly as any other listed company does; governance in a listed family managed company cannot be isolated from governance in a non-family business. The other three, along with the formation of a coterie, the dilution of control as shareholding passes down the generations, and leadership crises on the death or disability of a senior member, are the stated features.
topic_text: Features of family owned companies in India
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is identified as an emerging issue in the governance of family managed companies in India?

options.A: The promoter family gives up its shareholding altogether and retains only a supervisory presence on the Board of the company
options.B: Professional managers are progressively replaced by family members so that the leadership of the group remains united
options.C: The company avoids listing its shares so that the compliance burden imposed by the listing regulations never arises
options.D: The social and emotional aspirations of the family are met through trusts or foundations kept separate from the business entity

answer_html:
Answer: (D) The social and emotional aspirations of the family are met through trusts or foundations kept separate from the business entity.

Among the emerging issues are the separation of ownership from management, family members acquiring professional qualifications from reputed institutes, promoters encouraging professionals within the organisation, a sharper focus on compliance to avoid loss of reputation and a fall in the share price, clarity of role and leadership settled at Board level, owners honouring the opinion of managers, and the family's social and emotional issues being satisfied through separate trusts or foundations without any conflict of interest.
topic_text: Emerging issues in family managed companies

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following will NOT be considered corporate social responsibility expenditure?

options.A: A contribution made to a political party or for a political purpose
options.B: Promotion of skill development among the impoverished communities
options.C: Improvement of health, nutrition and sanitation in a backward region
options.D: Capacity building for the inclusive growth of the weaker sections

answer_html:
Answer: (A) A contribution made to a political party or for a political purpose.

The expenditure which shall not be considered CSR is publicity activity with the sole intention of advertising a product or service, compliance with a regulation or a Government order, employee and employee family benefits whether direct or indirect, anything done to the physical environment to facilitate production or distribution of goods, and any contribution to a political party or for a political purpose. Health, nutrition, sanitation, education, skill development and inclusive growth are all Schedule VII activities.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is an advantage of implementing a CSR project through a specialised implementing agency rather than directly?

options.A: The company obtains the expertise of the agency, an unbiased view and better supervision at the site
options.B: Decisions are quicker, because even the smallest decisions are taken within the company itself
options.C: Coordination with third parties is avoided altogether and the cost of the project is thereby reduced
options.D: The company retains full flexibility, the project being supervised by its own CSR department

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The company obtains the expertise of the agency, an unbiased view and better supervision at the site.

The advantages of third party implementation are the expertise of the agency, better supervision at the site, an unbiased view, a single point of coordination and the ability to negotiate cost. Flexibility, better internal supervision, quick decision making, the absence of coordination with third parties and lower cost are the advantages claimed for direct implementation by the company itself.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: To obtain a real picture of the impact of a completed CSR project, the impact analysis study should be-

options.A: made by the CSR committee itself, covering both the process followed and the expenditure
options.B: deferred for three years after the benefit is given, so that long term effects become visible
options.C: confined to a comparison of the amount sanctioned with the amount actually disbursed
options.D: made preferably by an independent agency, focused only on the impact and based on data

answer_html:
Answer: (D) made preferably by an independent agency, focused only on the impact and based on data.

Impact refers to the success of the activity in relation to the target and is confined to the target beneficiaries. The study compares the achieved result with the desired result, and to give a real picture it should preferably be done by an independent agency, be focused on the impact alone, be done immediately after the benefit is given, and be data based. It helps in formulating the future action plan, reviewing the policy and suggesting corrective action.
topic_text: Impact assessment of a CSR project

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Sahyadri Tyres Limited is a public company manufacturing tyres for all classes of vehicles, with three manufacturing units and a corporate office. The company is professionally managed: the promoter is the chairman, attends only Board meetings and does not interfere in day to day management, and the other directors are independent professionals.

The financial performance of the company for the four financial years ended 31 March 2025 is as follows, the figures being ₹ in crore.

Turnover - 2021-22: 640; 2022-23: 710; 2023-24: 880; 2024-25: 1,040.

Net worth - 2021-22: 380; 2022-23: 410; 2023-24: 445; 2024-25: 470.

Net profit - 2021-22: 15; 2022-23: 18; 2023-24: 20; 2024-25: 22.

The Board is considering the corporate social responsibility obligation of the company for the financial year 2025-26.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. On the financial results shown, the corporate social responsibility obligation under Section 135-

options.A: does not apply, because the net worth of ₹470 crore in the preceding financial year falls short of the threshold
options.B: applies, but only because the net worth of ₹470 crore taken with the turnover of ₹1,040 crore crosses the threshold
options.C: does not apply, because the section is attracted only where the net worth, turnover and net profit tests are all met
options.D: applies, the turnover of ₹1,040 crore and the net profit of ₹22 crore in the preceding year each attracting the section

answer_html:
Answer: (D) applies, the turnover of ₹1,040 crore and the net profit of ₹22 crore in the preceding year each attracting the section.

Section 135(1) applies to every company having a net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or a turnover of ₹1000 crore or more, or a net profit of ₹5 crore or more during the immediately preceding financial year. The three tests are alternatives, so satisfying any one of them is enough. For 2024-25 the turnover of ₹1,040 crore and the net profit of ₹22 crore each cross their thresholds; the net worth of ₹470 crore does not, but that is immaterial.

question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The minimum amount which Sahyadri Tyres Limited must spend on corporate social responsibility in 2025-26 is-

options.A: ₹35.33 lakh
options.B: ₹40.00 lakh
options.C: ₹44.00 lakh
options.D: ₹37.50 lakh

answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹40.00 lakh.

The company must spend at least two per cent of the average net profit of the three immediately preceding financial years, that is 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25. The average is ₹18 crore plus ₹20 crore plus ₹22 crore divided by three, which is ₹20 crore, and two per cent of that is ₹40.00 lakh. Taking the latest year alone gives ₹44.00 lakh, averaging all four years gives ₹37.50 lakh, and averaging the three years up to 2023-24 gives ₹35.33 lakh.

question_html: Refer to the case scenario. As regards the constitution of a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee, the correct position is that-

options.A: no such committee need be constituted, because the company is professionally managed and its chairman takes no part in the management
options.B: a committee must be constituted, but it may be composed entirely of the independent directors who are already on the Board
options.C: no such committee need be constituted, the amount to be spent not exceeding ₹50 lakh, and the Board will discharge its functions
options.D: a committee of three or more directors, at least one of them independent, must be constituted in every case where the section applies

answer_html:
Answer: (C) no such committee need be constituted, the amount to be spent not exceeding ₹50 lakh, and the Board will discharge its functions.

Where the amount required to be spent does not exceed ₹50 lakh the requirement of constituting a CSR Committee does not apply, and the functions of that committee are discharged by the Board of Directors of the company. The amount here is ₹40.00 lakh, so no committee is needed. The professional character of the management and the composition of the Board have no bearing on the question.

question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Of the amount required to be spent for 2025-26, ₹12 lakh remains unspent at the end of the year and relates to an ongoing project. That amount has to be spent within-

options.A: three financial years succeeding the financial year in which it remained unspent
options.B: one financial year succeeding the financial year in which it remained unspent
options.C: two financial years succeeding the financial year in which it remained unspent
options.D: four financial years succeeding the financial year in which it remained unspent

answer_html:
Answer: (A) three financial years succeeding the financial year in which it remained unspent.

An amount earmarked for an ongoing project which remains unspent must be spent within three financial years. The concession is confined to an ongoing project; an amount unspent otherwise than in respect of an ongoing project does not get the benefit of that period.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: In the triple bottom line approach to sustainable development, the ecological or environmental approach is described as the-

options.A: Purpose approach
options.B: Planet approach
options.C: Profit approach
options.D: People approach

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Planet approach.

The three approaches are the economic approach, under which the current decision should not impair the prospects of maintaining or improving future living standards, called the Profit approach; the ecological or environmental approach, requiring scarce natural resources to be preserved, called the Planet approach; and the social approach, requiring that social security, values and welfare are not damaged, called the People approach. Together they are known as the three P approach.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Sustainable development was defined in the report Our Common Future, which was released by-

options.A: the United Nations General Assembly in 2015
options.B: the World Bank Group in the year 1992
options.C: the UN Human Rights Council in 2011
options.D: the Brundtland Commission in 1987

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the Brundtland Commission in 1987.

Sustainable development is the development of processes by which the needs of the present are met without harming the ability of the future to meet its own needs, as defined in the report Our Common Future, commonly known as the Brundtland Report, released by the Brundtland Commission in 1987. The 2030 Agenda with its seventeen Sustainable Development Goals came from the UN General Assembly in September 2015.
topic_text: Origin of the definition of sustainable development

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, the format for which was prescribed by SEBI in May 2021-

options.A: is voluntary for all listed companies, the Annual Business Responsibility Report remaining the mandatory one
options.B: is mandatory for every company to which the corporate social responsibility provisions apply, listed or not
options.C: is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23 for the top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation
options.D: is mandatory from the financial year 2021-22 for the top 500 listed companies by market capitalisation

answer_html:
Answer: (C) is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23 for the top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation.

SEBI first prescribed a format for reporting environmental, social and governance parameters in November 2015 and revised it in May 2021 as the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, which seeks disclosure by listed entities of their performance against the principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct. Filing is mandatory with effect from the financial year 2022-23 for the top 1000 companies listed on any exchange, measured by market capitalisation.
source_file: CMA FINAL Paper 13 corporate laws Dec26.pdf

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Each parameter of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report is divided into leadership indicators and essential indicators. The position is that-

options.A: both sets of indicators are voluntary, the report being wholly a matter of self-regulation
options.B: the leadership indicators are voluntary while the essential indicators are mandatory
options.C: the leadership indicators are mandatory while the essential indicators are voluntary
options.D: both sets of indicators are mandatory for every listed entity required to file the report

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the leadership indicators are voluntary while the essential indicators are mandatory.

In the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report each parameter is divided into leadership indicators and essential indicators, the former being voluntary and the latter mandatory. The purpose of the disclosure is to present information of a quantity and standard which permits ready comparison with similar entities, particularly by a prospective investor, to engage with stakeholders, and to make corporates look beyond financial figures.
